reviewedContributions.name: Personal & Professional Development

evidence.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
evidence.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.

reviewedContributions.name: Introduction to Data Science

evidence.description2: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
evidence.profile: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.

reviewedContributions.finding: Importing, cleaning, joining and visualising tabular/spatial data in R and a data research project directly support biological data analysis.

reviewedContributions.name: Machine Learning

evidence.description2: Covers core machine learning techniques from linear regression to advanced tree‑based methods. Discusses strengths and weaknesses and applies methods to real data from fields like medicine, physics and economics.
evidence.profile: Introduces statistical learning for understanding data and predicting outcomes. Students study regression and classification, model accuracy, resampling, regularization, nonlinear models, trees, support vector machines and unsupervised learning. Practical assignments evaluate methods on real data using R or Python. Projects emphasize informative predictor construction, test-set prediction, appropriate model choice and clear reporting of results and limitations.

reviewedContributions.name: Image Processing & Computer Vision

evidence.description2: Covers processing and analysis of image data, including feature detection and tracking. Discusses applications in medicine, self‑driving vehicles, gaming, robotics and traffic management.
evidence.profile: Examines how digital images are represented, processed and interpreted to recognize structures and objects. Spatial and spectral representations, colour and image statistics support filtering, segmentation, curve and feature detection, tracking and object classification. Students use Python and OpenCV to implement image-processing techniques, investigate spectral representations, and build a recognition pipeline whose performance is benchmarked on previously unseen images.

reviewedContributions.name: Neural Networks & Deep Learning

evidence.description2: Explores theory and practice of neural networks. Students build basic networks and progress to complex networks for computer vision, and discuss recent developments in large language and image generation models.
evidence.profile: Develops neural-network theory and practical implementation in Python, Keras and TensorFlow. Students build and train simple networks before studying multilayer architectures, backpropagation, regularization and model evaluation. Later work applies deep learning to computer vision, time series and text, including transformers. Projects construct predictors for tabular data and investigate an independently chosen image- or text-based prediction problem, with experimental results reported in a paper.

reviewedContributions.name: Introduction to Programming

evidence.description2: Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and develops computational problem‑solving skills.
evidence.profile: Introduces computational problem-solving and programming in Python. Students develop structured programs using branching, iteration, functions and data collections, then progress to recursion, exception handling and object-oriented programming with inheritance. Elements of logic, sets and enumeration support computational reasoning. Exercises and projects require students to write, trace, test, debug and explain programs that solve problems of moderate complexity.

reviewedContributions.name: Mathematical Methods

evidence.description2: Introduces linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) and calculus (limits, differentiation, integration) to construct and solve equations. Provides problem‑solving skills applicable across disciplines.
evidence.profile: Develops single-variable calculus and related mathematical tools for modelling scientific problems. Functions, limits and differentiation lead to optimization, Taylor series, complex numbers, integration and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica, including numerical approximation. A project implements, analyzes and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and explanation of the computational results.

reviewedContributions.name: Probability & Statistics

evidence.description2: Provides a foundation in mathematical statistics. Covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; uses computer algebra software to develop theoretical understanding and practical skills.
evidence.profile: Provides a rigorous introduction to probability and mathematical statistics, from probability spaces and random variables to multivariate distributions and statistical inference. Students study estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and maximum-likelihood methods, followed by an introduction to Bayesian reasoning. Mathematica simulations verify analytical results. A substantial project implements and compares random-sampling algorithms, including inverse sampling, accept-reject sampling and Gibbs sampling.

reviewedContributions.name: Introduction to Biodiversity

evidence.description2: The biosphere consists of millions of living species. In this course we will travel through the tree of life, starting with bacteria and single-celled eukaryotes such as reef-building dinoflagellates and disease-causing apicomplexans. Next, we will look at the multicellular groups: plants, seaweeds, fungi and animals. We will also investigate the relevance of biodiversity for human society in fields such as food and food security, economy, climate and health.
evidence.profile: Surveys the diversity and evolutionary relationships of living organisms across the tree of life. Students examine prokaryotes, protists, fungi, plants and animals, their distinguishing characteristics and ecological roles. Practical work introduces microscopy, organism identification and biodiversity measurement. A small project investigates a selected phylogenetic branch, supported by literature searching, data collection and analysis.
evidence.topics: Biodiversity and its measurement; Phylogenetic relationships; Viruses; Bacteria and archaea; Protists; Fungi; Plant diversity; Invertebrates; Vertebrates and primates; Evolutionary history; Organismal ecological roles
evidence.methods: Microscopy; Organism identification using identification apps; Rank-abundance diagrams; Species-saturation curves; Biodiversity indices; Phylogenetic research; Scholarly database searching; Biodiversity data collection and analysis

reviewedContributions.finding: Surveys the tree of life, microorganisms, plants, animals and methods for investigating biodiversity.

reviewedContributions.name: Conservation Biology

evidence.description2: This course explores environmental conservation through biological and social science perspectives. Topics include biodiversity importance, threats to ecosystems, conservation methods, and tools to monitor and protect nature. It also covers national and international laws, policies, and initiatives aimed at preserving ecosystems and ensuring a sustainable future for current and future generations.
evidence.profile: Introduces conservation biology through biodiversity loss, its human causes and possible responses. Students examine habitat destruction and fragmentation, overharvesting, invasive species, climate change, disasters and extinction, followed by conservation planning, species management and conservation in altered landscapes. A local threatened-species project investigates conservation status and protection measures and develops a public-awareness flyer.

reviewedContributions.finding: Examines extinction, human impacts and scientific and policy responses in conservation biology.

reviewedContributions.name: The Science of Evolution

evidence.description2: Evolution is the unifying theory in biology. As such, an understanding of evolutionary biology is vital for understanding the natural world. In this course, we will discuss key concepts in evolution such as population genetics, variation and selection, speciation, macro-evolution and the origins of life. The importance of evolutionary concepts to all other fields of biology will be emphasized, as well as important implications of evolutionary processes in fields like human health and climate change.
evidence.profile: Examines evolutionary theory from genetic mechanisms to the diversification and history of life. Students study natural selection, variation and drift, population and quantitative genetics, adaptation and sexual reproduction, then species concepts, speciation, phylogeny and macroevolution. Genomics, development, biogeography and coevolution extend the account across scales. A project reconstructs a chosen species' evolutionary history using Tinbergen's four questions.

evidence.methods: Evolutionary-history analysis using Tinbergen's four questions; Phylogenetic reconstruction

reviewedContributions.finding: Studies evolutionary mechanisms from genes to populations and their application across biology.

reviewedContributions.name: Ecosystems Uncovered: How Nature Works

evidence.description2: Focuses on basic principles of ecology. Studies how environmental conditions affect organisms and examines ecological principles governing individuals, populations, communities and ecosystems, including ecological modelling and applied case studies.
evidence.profile: Develops ecological principles from organisms and populations to communities and ecosystems. Environmental conditions, resources and life cycles frame competition, feeding relationships, selection, population dynamics and biodiversity. Energy and matter cycles connect ecological processes to conservation and human impacts. Dedicated practical sessions teach simple ecological modelling in R, and a small research project communicates findings through a poster.

reviewedContributions.name: Marine Biology

evidence.profile: Examines marine ecological processes, ocean systems and human impacts on the sea. Physical and chemical oceanography support the study of primary and secondary production, microbial ecology, and habitats from estuaries and shores to the open ocean, deep sea and polar regions. Student seminars address fisheries, aquaculture, acidification, sea-level rise and plastic pollution. A multimedia outreach project translates a marine biological topic for a public audience.

A literature-based project critically investigates a chosen sustainable-farming question and reports the evidence without prescribing a single preferred approach.

reviewedContributions.name: Soils & Aquifers

Soil formation, functions, quality and threats connect to texture, structure, composition, biological activity and salinization. Field sampling and laboratory investigations characterize soil properties and sediment-cell behaviour. Seismic, electrical-resistivity and electromagnetic surveys investigate physical and geophysical properties of soils and aquifers. Students document procedures and observations, process field data in Excel, interpret results and develop evidence-based field and laboratory reports.

reviewedContributions.name: Climate Change

evidence.description2: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. reviewedContributions.name: Pharmacology

Applications emphasize nervous-system drugs, antimicrobial treatment and inflammatory, immune and airway conditions. Quantitative exercises and virtual experiments model drug responses, while a psychoactive-drug project proposes a testable follow-up experiment.

reviewedContributions.name: Psycholinguistics

evidence.description2: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.

reviewedContributions.finding: Neural signalling, brain development, learning and combined behavioural/imaging/electrophysiological approaches complement the study of animal behaviour and neurobiology; not a replacement for organismal zoology.

reviewedContributions.name: Molecular Cell Biology

evidence.description2: Provides foundation for practical applications in life science. Focuses on cellular biology of eukaryotes and prokaryotes, revisits concepts from introductory courses, examines current research and encourages evaluating reproducibility and modernising methods.
evidence.profile: Studies the molecular mechanisms underlying cellular structure, physiology and regulation, primarily in eukaryotes. Bioenergetics, proteins and membranes connect to genome replication, repair and gene expression, followed by trafficking, signalling, division, tissues, stem cells and cancer. Students evaluate research methods and reproducibility and investigate a drug's molecular target, therapeutic action, metabolism and adverse effects through primary literature, a paper and a research poster.
evidence.topics: Cellular components and bioenergetics; Proteins and membranes; Cytoskeleton; DNA replication and repair; Genomes; Regulation of gene expression; Membrane transport and trafficking; Cell-signalling pathways; Cell division and fate; Tissue organization; Stem cells; Cancer; Molecular mechanisms of drug action
evidence.methods: Critical analysis of primary molecular-biology literature; Evaluation of research-method limitations and reproducibility; Thermodynamic free-energy calculations; Molecular mechanism analysis

reviewedContributions.finding: Develops molecular-cell biology, genomes, gene expression, signalling, division, tissues and current research methods.

reviewedContributions.name: Human Physiology

evidence.description2: Studies normal functioning of the human body, covering structure‑function relationships, energy handling, homeostasis, signalling, organ systems and integration of their functions.
evidence.profile: Studies normal function and regulation in the adult human body, linking molecular and cellular processes to integrated organ systems. Homeostasis, signalling and energy handling frame nervous, endocrine, muscular, respiratory, cardiovascular, renal, digestive and reproductive functions. Medical examples illustrate physiological principles. An individual literature-based paper examines a selected physiological or pathophysiological process and is developed through structured peer review and revision.
evidence.topics: Cells, tissues and membrane dynamics; Homeostasis and control; Cellular signalling; Endocrine and nervous regulation; Muscles and movement; Breathing and gas exchange; Blood and cardiovascular function; Renal function; Fluid and electrolyte balance; Digestion and metabolism; Growth and exercise physiology; Reproduction and development
evidence.methods: Physiological literature review; Medline/PubMed literature searching; Scientific peer review and evidence-based revision

reviewedContributions.finding: Examines molecules, cells, tissues, organ systems, homeostasis and organismal physiology.

reviewedContributions.name: Biochemistry

evidence.description2: Explores the chemistry of life and biomolecules such as proteins, sugars, lipids and nucleic acids. Discusses metabolic pathways, the role of biomolecules in health and disease and applications in medicine, biotechnology and sustainability.
evidence.profile: Examines the chemistry of life, emphasizing biomolecular structure and function, enzymes and metabolic pathways. Students study proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, enzyme kinetics and regulation, glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, the citric-acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation and further carbohydrate, lipid and nitrogen metabolism. Protein-biochemistry techniques are discussed. A literature-based disease project links a biochemical defect to symptoms, diagnostics and treatment, keeping the molecular mechanism central.
evidence.topics: Water and weak bonds; Amino acids and protein structure; Protein-biochemistry techniques; Enzyme action, kinetics, regulation and inhibition; Hemoglobin; Carbohydrates and lipids; Metabolic organization; Glycolysis and gluconeogenesis; Citric-acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation; Glycogen and pentose-phosphate metabolism; Fatty-acid and lipid metabolism; Nitrogen and urea cycle; Biochemical mechanisms of disease
evidence.methods: Biochemical pathway and disease-mechanism analysis; Primary-literature review

reviewedContributions.finding: Covers biomolecules, metabolism, signalling and biochemical foundations of biotechnology and disease.

reviewedContributions.name: Life Science Laboratory

evidence.description2: Introduces biochemical and molecular laboratory work. Covers themes like blood, proteins, bacteria, DNA and bioinformatics and provides a foundation for clinical and biomedical research.
evidence.profile: Provides hands-on training in biochemical, microbiological and molecular laboratory methods. Blood analysis, microbial culture and hygiene lead into bacterial transformation, green fluorescent protein production and purification, DNA isolation and analysis, and introductory bioinformatics. Students follow and sometimes adapt protocols, interpret experimental results, maintain reproducible laboratory records and communicate findings in scientific reports and figures.
evidence.topics: Blood cells and proteins; Blood groups and hemograms; Aseptic culture and bacterial identification; Disinfection and sterilization; Antibiotic susceptibility; Genetically modified bacteria; GFP production and purification; DNA and plasmid analysis; PCR and restriction digestion; Protein and DNA databases; Genotype and population-genetic interpretation; Experimental reproducibility
evidence.methods: Pipetting and workflow planning; Microscopy and blood-smear examination; Blood cell counting and hemogram measurement; ELISA; Aseptic culture and purity streaking; Bacterial identification and inhibition-zone testing; Sterilization and disinfection testing; pGLO bacterial transformation; Protein extraction and chromatographic purification; SDS-PAGE; DNA and plasmid isolation; PCR; Restriction digestion and agarose-gel electrophoresis; DNA and protein database searching; Laboratory notebook and scientific-report preparation

reviewedContributions.finding: Provides molecular and microbiological laboratory work, including proteins, PCR, electrophoresis and bioinformatics.

reviewedContributions.name: Molecular Pathology & Genetics

evidence.description2: Covers general and molecular pathology and genetics. Studies cell injury, death, inflammation, immunity, tissue repair, regeneration, fibrosis and neoplasia, examines genetic mutations and diseases, and discusses genetic testing and ethical considerations.
evidence.profile: Connects cellular pathology with the genetic mechanisms of human disease. Students examine injury and death, inflammation and repair, neoplasia and lymphoid malignancies, then inheritance, genetic variation, epigenetics, molecular diagnosis and genetic treatment. Ethical, legal and safety questions accompany genetic technologies. A two-year research-grant proposal integrates literature, hypotheses, method selection, controls, feasibility and budgeting; an ethics debate examines stakeholder positions.
evidence.topics: Cell injury, adaptation and death; Acute and chronic inflammation; Regeneration, repair and fibrosis; Neoplasia; Pulmonary pathology; Leukemia and lymphoma; Genes, genomes and inheritance; Genetic variation and chromosome abnormalities; Gene regulation and epigenetics; Genotype-phenotype relationships; Genetic testing and DNA technologies; Gene-based therapies and cell manipulation; Genetics ethics, law and biosafety
evidence.methods: Biomedical literature review; Research-grant proposal design; Hypothesis formulation and experimental-control selection; Research feasibility, timeline and budget planning; Stakeholder-based ethical argument analysis

reviewedContributions.finding: Advances molecular genetics, mutation, inheritance, pathology, testing and treatment.

findings: Four old hard conflicts repaired: deep-learning offering, Psycholinguistics offering, HumanPhysiology earlier prerequisite and delta-research offering. No old offering is restored. Neurobiological language evidence is fully considered from description2 and scheduled2027spring afterBrain/Behaviour. No outline absence exclusion.

Removed generic governance/hazards and open-ended delta-project framing where it did not implement defining biological study. Strengthened actual experimental biology, evolution, environmental chemistry, data handling and biological cognition. Ecology candidate retains genetics/physiology as biological foundations while prioritising ecological systems; four unique courses against broad route are curricular consequences, not arbitrary numerical swaps.

Human-focused biomedical courses are not plant/animal general equivalents. General ML/image/deep-learning are data-method complements, not biological neural circuitry. Shared methods alone do not force external alignment. Removed PPD-to-disciplinary-ethics match; added stronger gene/protein laboratory, genetics and evolution relationships with bounded scope. Meaningful blanks and optional research outside180 remain explicit. Full comparability is conditional on valid external choices.
